# Exact transfer of simplex enclosure defects through Minkowski sums

Throughout, `|E|` denotes d-dimensional Lebesgue volume and d>=1.
All bodies in this note are compact convex sets with nonempty interior
in R^d. For nonnegative scalars, sums of bodies mean Minkowski sums;
`0 A={0}`. The statements concern ordinary continuous volume only.
They do not assert a mixed-integer centerpoint or a selection theorem.

## 1. Parallel simplex enclosures and the exact transfer inequality

Let A_1,...,A_N be bodies, let lambda_i>=0 with at least one positive
lambda_i, and put

    K=sum_i lambda_i A_i.

Let S be any full-dimensional simplex containing K whose every facet
supports K. Choose outward facet normals u_0,...,u_d, with arbitrary
positive normalizations, and define

    P_i={x:u_j.x<=h_(A_i)(u_j), j=0,...,d}.        (1)

Here h_A(u)=max_(x in A) u.x is the support function. Then every P_i
is a full-dimensional translated positive homothet of S, contains A_i,
and satisfies

    sum_i lambda_i P_i=S.                        (2)

Moreover,

    sum_i lambda_i^d (|P_i|-|A_i|)
                       <=|S|-|K|.               (3)

In particular the assertion holds for every minimum-volume enclosing
simplex of K. Such a minimizer exists and all its facets support K,
as proved in `candidate 783495094e97ee67`.

### Proof of the geometric claims

Choose an invertible LINEAR map L sending the facet directions of S
to those of T=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d). Such a map is the linear part of
an affine map sending S to T; thus LS is a translate of T. Apply L
to every body, including S. Linear maps commute with all the weighted
Minkowski sums here and multiply every volume in (3) by the same
positive absolute determinant. No translation is applied to the
summands in this normalization. In particular there is no implicit
assumption that sum_i lambda_i=1. This is a purely continuous change
of coordinates, with no lattice preservation assertion.

In these coordinates write

    P_i={x:x_k>=a_(ik), sum_k x_k<=b_i},
    a_(ik)=min_(x in A_i) x_k,
    b_i=max_(x in A_i) sum_k x_k,
    r_i=b_i-sum_k a_(ik).

The inclusion A_i subset P_i follows directly from the definitions.
Since A_i has interior, r_i>0: otherwise every point satisfying these
inequalities would have all coordinates equal to their lower bounds.
The displayed region is exactly

    P_i=a_i+r_i T.                               (4)

Thus it is a full-dimensional simplex, all its listed planes are
actual facets, and it is a positive homothet of S up to translation.
Minkowski addition of these parallel simplices gives

    sum_i lambda_i P_i
      =(sum_i lambda_i a_i)+(sum_i lambda_i r_i)T. (5)

The minimum of each coordinate on K and the maximum of their sum
are respectively sum_i lambda_i a_(ik) and sum_i lambda_i b_i:
each extremum separates into independent extrema over the summands.
Because every facet of S supports K, these are exactly the facet
offsets defining S. Equation (5) is therefore S, proving (2).

### Proof of the volume inequality

We use the standard Minkowski polynomial and monotonicity theorem
for mixed volumes. In the convention V_d(A,...,A)=|A|, these say

    |sum_i t_i B_i|
      =sum_(alpha_1+...+alpha_N=d)
          d!/(alpha_1!...alpha_N!) product_i t_i^(alpha_i)
          V_d(B_1[alpha_1],...,B_N[alpha_N]),     (6)

for t_i>=0, and the mixed volume is monotone in each body argument
under inclusion. An argument of multiplicity zero is omitted.
These are ordinary mixed-volume facts for compact convex bodies;
no mixed-integer inequality is being invoked.

For every multi-index alpha, inclusion A_i subset P_i and repeated
monotonicity give

    V_d(P_1[alpha_1],...,P_N[alpha_N])
       -V_d(A_1[alpha_1],...,A_N[alpha_N])>=0.    (7)

Subtract (6) for the two collections at t_i=lambda_i. By (2) the
left side is |S|-|K|. Retain only the pure multi-indices alpha=d e_i.
Their coefficients are lambda_i^d and their mixed volumes are the
ordinary volumes |P_i| and |A_i|. Every omitted term is nonnegative
by (7). This is exactly (3). All sums are finite. Zero weights cause
no difficulty: terms involving a positive power of such a weight
vanish, or the zero-weight summands may simply be removed in advance.

Translations do not affect mixed volumes. In particular individual
summands need not contain the origin, and no signed support-function
comparison is required in (7).

There is a useful dimensionless version. In (4), put
R_0=sum_i lambda_i r_i>0, alpha_i=lambda_i r_i/R_0, and
delta_i=1-|A_i|/|P_i|. Then alpha_i>=0 and sum_i alpha_i=1.
Since |P_i|=r_i^d |T| and |S|=R_0^d |T|, (3) is exactly

    sum_i alpha_i^d delta_i <=1-|K|/|S|.         (3a)

In particular, if K itself is a simplex, every A_i with positive
lambda_i is a simplex homothetic to K: choose S=K, so (3) forces
|P_i|=|A_i|. Inclusion of full-dimensional compact convex bodies
and equality of volumes then force P_i=A_i. To justify the last
step, a point in P_i outside A_i is strictly separated from A_i;
its cone to an interior ball of A_i contains positive volume beyond
the separating plane, contradicting equal volumes.

## 2. A containing middle body: the volume slack must remain

Suppose Q is any body containing K, and now take S to be a
minimum-volume enclosing simplex of Q. Define P_i by (1), using
the normals of this S. Every P_i still has the form (4). The sum

    R=sum_i lambda_i P_i

is the simplex in those directions whose facets have offsets
h_K(u_j). In particular K subset R subset S, because
h_K(u_j)<=h_Q(u_j). The preceding polynomial argument gives

    sum_i lambda_i^d (|P_i|-|A_i|)
       <=|R|-|K|
       <= (|S|-|Q|)+(|Q|-|K|).                  (8)

This preserves the additional volume of Q beyond the Minkowski sum.
It is not permissible to drop the second term merely because Q
contains K. When Q=K, R=S and (8) reduces to (3).

## 3. Conversion of ordinary depth stability to an absolute budget

For a body Q define its normalized maximum ordinary halfspace depth

    D(Q)=max_(y in Q) inf_(closed halfspaces H containing y)
                                      |Q intersect H|/|Q|,
    Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d.

For d>=2, `candidate 3787afd8b1ed0167`
proves a finite constant A_d, depending only on d, such that every
minimum enclosing simplex S of Q satisfies

    (|S|-|Q|)/|S| <= A_d [D(Q)-Gamma_d].         (9)

There is also the elementary uniform volume comparison

    |S| <= (d+2)^d |Q|.                         (10)

For completeness, choose a maximum-volume inscribed simplex T_0
in Q. It exists by continuity of the determinant on the compact
set Q^(d+1), and it has positive volume. Send it affinely to
T=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d). Write lambda_0,...,lambda_d for the affine
barycentric coordinates with sum 1. For any x in Q, replacing
the j-th vertex of T by x produces an inscribed simplex of volume
|lambda_j(x)||T|. Maximality gives |lambda_j(x)|<=1. Consequently

    Q subset U={x:lambda_j(x)>=-1 for all j}.

This U is a simplex. The coordinates
(lambda_j+1)/(d+2) are nonnegative and sum to 1, so U is a translated
homothet of T with ratio d+2. Thus |U|=(d+2)^d |T|. Minimality
of S and T subset Q yield (10). The argument is affine invariant.

Combining (8)-(10) gives the absolute-error estimate

    sum_i lambda_i^d (|P_i|-|A_i|)
       <= A_d (d+2)^d |Q| [D(Q)-Gamma_d]
                                      +|Q|-|K|. (11)

For Q=K the last term is zero. For d=1 all bodies are intervals,
and the two supporting directions enclose each A_i exactly, so
the left sides of (3), (8), and (11) are zero. No higher-dimensional
formula for A_d is needed in that case.

When Q=K, (3a) and (9) also give the sharper scale-aware estimate

    sum_i alpha_i^d delta_i <=A_d[D(K)-Gamma_d]. (11a)

This bounds every positive-scale summand separately by division
by alpha_i^d; no positive lower bound on these scales is assumed.

## 4. Exact sharpness of the coefficient in (3)

For every d>=2 the coefficient 1 in (3) is attained with two
full-dimensional summands of positive weights. We first verify
the minimum-simplex fact needed for an explicit example.

Let

    T=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d),
    A_e={x in T:sum_j x_j>=e},
    0<e<=1/(64 d^4).                            (12)

Then T is the UNIQUE minimum-volume enclosing simplex of A_e.
Indeed the infinity-norm Hausdorff distance between A_e and T is
e/d: a point with coordinate sum s<e can be moved by
((e-s)/d)(1,...,1), and the origin has distance at least e/d
from A_e. The contact/locality theorem in the cited minimum-simplex
note therefore says that every minimizing simplex S_e has its
vertices, after the reference labeling, within

    8 d^3(e/d)=8 d^2 e <=1/(8 d^2)             (13)

of the corresponding vertices of T. The theorem's hypotheses
hold since e/d<=1/(64 d^3). Its facet centroids are actual points
of A_e and satisfy the same distance estimate from the corresponding
facet centroids of T.

Let p be the centroid of the facet of S_e corresponding to a
facet F_i of T, and put rho=1/(8d^2). At the centroid of F_i,
each barycentric coordinate other than lambda_i is 1/d. Each
coordinate lambda_j with j>=1 changes by at most rho on a rho
infinity ball, while lambda_0=1-sum_j x_j changes by at most
d rho. Therefore at p all the other barycentric coordinates
are at least

    1/d-d rho=7/(8d)>0.                         (14)

Furthermore the coordinate sum at p is at least
(d-1)/d-d rho=(d-1)/d-1/(8d), whether i=0 or i>=1;
this exceeds e for d>=2 and e as in (12). Thus the truncating
plane sum x_j=e does not meet any of these contact neighborhoods.

Because p lies in A_e and on the boundary of S_e while A_e subset
S_e, it belongs to the boundary of A_e. By (14) and the strict
truncation inequality, the only boundary plane of A_e at p can
be the original facet plane F_i. In fact p lies in the relative
interior of F_i. A convex body has a unique supporting hyperplane
at a point in the relative interior of one of its facets when
all its other defining inequalities are strict: a small relative
ball in that plane, together with a point strictly inside the
body, forces any supporting functional to be a positive multiple
of the facet's outward normal. The plane of the selected S_e
facet must therefore be exactly the plane of F_i. This applies
to all d+1 facets, proving S_e=T and uniqueness.

Now take any t>0 and B=tT. Directly,

    A_e+B={x:x_j>=0, e<=sum_j x_j<=1+t}.         (15)

The inclusion from left to right is immediate. Conversely, if
x has sum s in [e,1+t], choose a scalar a in
[e,1] intersect [s-t,s], which is nonempty, and decompose
x=(a/s)x+(1-a/s)x. The first point is in A_e and the second
in tT. Here s>=e>0, so the formula is well defined.

After scaling (15) by 1/(1+t), its normalized truncation parameter
is e/(1+t), still within (12). Thus its unique minimum enclosing
simplex is S=(1+t)T. The simplices from (1) are P_A=T and P_B=tT.
Since the removed corner has volume e^d |T|,

    |P_A|-|A_e|=e^d |T|,
    |P_B|-|B|=0,
    |S|-|A_e+B|=e^d |T|.                        (16)

Equality holds in (3), with two positive coefficients lambda_A=
lambda_B=1. If coefficients are required to sum to 1, use 1/2,
1/2; both sides scale by 2^(-d), and equality remains exact.
Thus the factor 1 cannot be decreased, even with fixed positive
weights on two full-dimensional bodies.

The example also identifies why all cross mixed-volume defects
can vanish: for arbitrary a,b>0,

    |a A_e+b(tT)|=[(a+bt)^d-(ae)^d]|T|,

so the volume polynomial differs from that of aT+b(tT) only
in its pure a^d coefficient. The same identity extends to
a=0 by continuity.

## 5. Scope

The transfer is exact for every d, every finite number of summands,
and every set of nonnegative weights with a positive total. The
sharpness assertion is nonvacuous for d>=2; in d=1 all defects vanish.
The depth-stability input in (9) is kept separate from the elementary
transfer in (3), and (11) retains all volume slack of a containing
body. No conclusion about finding one mixed-integer point follows
from these estimates alone.
